    MA3003 · HEAT TRANSFER

    1D Steady Heat Conduction

    #Conduction in Plane Walls

    Consider steady heat conduction through a wall. Energy balance for the wall can be expressed as,

    dtdEwall​​=Q˙​in​−Q˙​out​

    Note that there is no heat generation.

    Since the heat transfer is a steady-state process,

    dtdEwall​​=0 ⟶ Q˙​in​=Q˙​out​

    Rate of heat transfer into the wall must be
    equal to the rate of heat transfer out of it.

    Thus, rate of heat transfer through the wall
    must be a constant, Q˙​cond,wall​=const.

    #Thermal Resistance Concept

    Ohm’s law is given by I=RV​.

    #Conduction Resistance

    From Fourier’s law of heat conduction,

    Q˙​cond​=−kAdxdT​

    Q˙​cond​=kALT1​−T2​​

    💡
    Q˙​cond​=L/kAT1​−T2​​=Rwall​T1​−T2​​

    where Rwall​ is the thermal resistance of the wall against heat conduction

    #Convection Resistance

    From Newton’s law of cooling,

    Q˙​conv​=hAs​(Ts​−T∞​)

    💡
    Q˙​conv​=1/hAs​Ts​−T∞​​=Rconv​Ts​−T∞​​

    where Rconv​ is the thermal resistance of a surface against heat convection

    Note that when the convection heat transfer coefficient h is very large, h→∞,
    the convection resistance becomes zero and     Ts​≈T∞​. Thus, the surface has no
    resistance to convection and does not slow down the heat transfer process.

    #Radiation Resistance

    Similarly for net radiation exchange,

    Q˙​rad​=εσAs​(Ts​4−Tsurr​4)

    Q˙​rad​=hrad​As​(Ts​−Tsurr​)

    💡
    Q˙​rad​=1/hrad​As​Ts​−Tsurr​​=Rrad​Ts​−Tsurr​​

    where Rrad​ is the thermal resistance of a surface against radiation

    Radiation heat transfer coefficient is defined as,

    💡
    hrad​=As​(Ts​−Tsurr​)Q˙​rad​​=εσ(Ts​2+Tsurr​2)(Ts​+Tsurr​)

    where the coefficient has S.I. units W/m2⋅K

    When Tsurr​≈T∞​, radiation is accounted for by,

    💡
    hcomb​=hconv​+hrad​

    The combined coefficient will then replace
    the     h in the convection resistance equation.

    #Thermal Resistance Circuit

    Consider a steady 1D heat transfer through a plane wall of thickness L and area A,
    with a constant thermal conductivity k that is exposed to convection on both sides.

    Energy balance for the wall is,

    Q˙​conv,1​=Q˙​cond​=Q˙​conv,2​

    h1​A(T∞1​​−T1​)=kALT1​−T2​​=h2​A(T2​−T∞2​​)

    1/h1​AT∞1​​−T1​​=L/kAT1​−T2​​=1/h2​AT2​−T∞2​​​

    Rconv,1​T∞1​​−T1​​=Rcond​T1​−T2​​=Rconv,2​T2​−T∞2​​​

    Adding the numerators and denominators,

    💡
    Q˙​=Rtotal​T∞1​​−T∞2​​​=∑RΔT​

    Note that the thermal resistances are in series. Thus, total thermal resistance
    is the sum of the individual thermal resistances in the path of heat transfer.

    Ratio of temperature drop to thermal resistance across any layer is constant. Thus, temperature
    drop of any layer is proportional to the thermal resistance of that layer.

    It is sometimes convenient to express heat transfer
    as an equation similar to Newton’s law of cooling.

    💡
    Q˙​=∑RΔT​=UA⋅ΔT

    where U is the overall heat transfer coefficient

    #Multi-layer Plane Wall

    Consider a plane wall that consists of two layers.
    Rate of steady heat transfer is expressed as,

    Q˙​=Rtotal​T∞1​​−T∞2​​​

    Total thermal resistance of the wall is,

    Rtotal​=Rconv,1​+Rwall,1​+Rwall,2​+Rconv,2​

    Rtotal​=h1​A1​+k1​AL1​​+k2​AL2​​+h2​A1​

    Using the electrical analogy, resistances arranged in series will experience the
    same rate of steady heat transfer Q˙​. Thus, if Q˙​ is known, an unknown surface
    temperature at any surface or interface can be determined.

    💡
    Q˙​=R i−j​Ti​−Tj​​

    where i−j follows the direction of steady heat transfer,
    and     Ri−j​ is the thermal resistance between locations i and j

    Assuming T∞1​​ and T∞2​​ for the two-layer wall are known, we can compute Q˙​.
    The interface temperature T2​ between the two layers can be determined from,

    💡
    Q˙​=Rconv,1​+Rwall,1​T∞1​​−T2​​=1/h1​A+L1​/k1​AT∞1​​−T2​​

    Note that the thermal resistance concept is limited to systems through which the
    rate of heat transfer     Q˙​ remains constant; systems involving steady heat transfer
    with no heat generation within the medium.

    #Example 1

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1-dimensional heat transfer
    • Constant thermal conductivity k

    Heat transfer through the window is steady since the surface temperatures remain constant at the specified values.

    Convection resistance (inner surface),

    Ri​=h1​A1​=10(1.2)1​=0.08333 K/W

    Conduction resistance of glass pane,

    Rcond​=kAL​=0.78(1.2)0.008​=0.00855 K/W

    Convection resistance (outer surface),

    Ro​=h2​A1​=40(1.2)1​=0.02083 K/W

    Heat transfer is similar to a series circuit.

    Rtot​=Ri​+Rcond​+Ro​

    Rtot​=0.08333+0.00855+0.02083

    Rtot​=0.1127 K/W

    Steady rate of heat transfer,

    Q˙​=∑RΔT​=0.112720−(−10)​=266 W

    Inner surface temperature of glass pane,

    Q˙​=R i−j​Ti​−Tj​​

    266=0.08333(20+273)−T1​​

    T1​=270.83 K=−2.2°C

    #Example 2

    Convection resistance (inner surface),

    Ri​=h1​A1​=10(1.2)1​=0.08333 K/W

    Conduction resistance of glass pane,

    R1​=R3​=Rglass​=k1​AL​

    Rglass​=0.78(1.2)0.004​=0.00427 K/W

    Conduction resistance of air gap,

    Rair​=k2​AL​=0.026(1.2)0.01​=0.3205 K/W

    Convection resistance (outer surface),

    Ro​=h2​A1​=40(1.2)1​=0.02083 K/W

    Total series thermal resistance,

    Rtot​=Ri​+Rglass,1​+Rair​+Rglass,2​+Ro​

    Rtot​=0.08333+2(0.00427)+0.3205+0.02083

    Rtot​=0.4332 K/W

    Steady rate of heat transfer,

    Q˙​=∑RΔT​=0.433220−(−10)​=69.2 W

    Inner surface temperature of window,

    Q˙​=R i−j​Ti​−Tj​​

    69.2=0.08333(20+273)−T1​​

    T1​=287.23 K=14.2°C

    #Generalized Circuits

    The thermal resistance concept can be used to solve problems that
    involve parallel layers or combined series-parallel arrangements.

    Consider a composite wall with two parallel layers. The thermal resistance circuit can be represented
    as two parallel branches.

    Total heat transfer is the sum of
    heat transfers though each layer.

    Q˙​=Q˙​1​+Q˙​2​

    Q˙​=R1​T1​−T2​​+R2​T1​−T2​​

    Q˙​=(T1​−T2​)(R1​1​+R2​1​)

    Q˙​=Rtotal​T1​−T2​​

    Note that total thermal resistance is computed in
    the same manner as resistors arranged in parallel.

    Consider a combined series-parallel arrangement.

    Total heat transfer through the system is then,

    Q˙​=Rtotal​T1​−T∞​​

    Note that there is convection resistance on the
    right side of the wall. Thus,     T∞​ is used instead.

    Total thermal resistance is expressed as,

    Rtotal​=1/R1​+1/R2​1​+R3​+Rconv​

    where R1​, R2​, and R3​ are conduction resistances

    #Example

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1-dimensional heat transfer
    • Constant thermal conductivities
    • Radiation Heat transfer is negligible

    h1​=10 W/m2⋅K

    h2​=25 W/m2⋅K

    kfoam​=0.025 W/m⋅K

    kplaster​=0.22 W/m⋅K

    kbrick​=0.72 W/m⋅K

    Individual thermal resistances

    Inner wall convection resistance,

    Ri​=Rconv,1​=h1​A1​=10(0.25)1​=0.4 K/W

    Foam conduction resistance,

    R1​=Rfoam​=kAL​=0.026(0.25)0.03​=4.62 K/W

    Plaster conduction resistance (series),

    R2​=R6​=Rplaster,side​=kAL​=0.22(0.25)0.02​=0.36 K/W

    Plastic conduction resistance (parallel),

    R3​=R5​=Rplaster,center​=kAL​=0.22(0.015)0.16​=48.48 K/W

    Brick conduction resistance,

    R4​=Rbrick​=kAL​=0.72(0.22)0.16​=1.01 K/W

    Outer wall convection resistance,

    Ro​=Rconv,2​=h2​A1​=25(0.25)1​=0.16 K/W

    Total thermal resistance,

    Rtot​=Ri​+R1​+R2​+1/R3​+1/R4​+1/R5​1​+R6​+Ro​

    Rtot​=0.4+4.62+0.36+1/48.48+1/1.01+1/48.481​+0.36+0.16

    Rtot​=6.87 K/W

    Rate of steady heat transfer per brick,

    Q˙​=Rtot​T∞1​​−T∞2​​​

    Q˙​=6.8720−(−10)​

    Q˙​=4.37 W (per 0.25m2 surface area)

    Total rate of steady heat transfer,

    Q˙​tot​=Q˙​Awall​

    Q˙​tot​=4.37(3×5)

    Q˙​tot​=263 W

    #Thermal Contact Resistance

    In the analysis of multi-layer solids, we assumed “perfect contact” at the interface
    of two layers, which is only true if the surfaces are perfectly smooth and produce
    a perfect contact at each point.

    Consider heat transfer through two solids that are pressed against each other.
    Heat transfer through the interface is the sum of heat transfer through the
    contact points (conduction) and the gaps (radiation).

    Q˙​=Q˙​contact​+Q˙​gaps​

    Q˙​=htc​AΔTinterface​

    where A is the apparent interface area,
    and     ΔT is the effective temperature difference

    Thermal contact conductance is defined as,

    💡
    htc​=ΔTinterface​Q˙​/A​

    Thermal contact resistance is then,

    💡
    Rtc′′​=htc​1​=Q˙​/AΔTinterface​​

    Note that Rtc′′​ represents resistance for a unit area and has units m2⋅K/W.
    Thermal resistance for the entire interface is obtained by dividing     Rtc′′​ by A.

    Factors that affect thermal contact resistance:

    • Surface roughness
    • Material properties
    • Temperature and pressure at interface
    • Type of fluid trapped at the interface

    #Example

    Thermal contact resistance of plates,

    Rtc′′​=htc​1​=180001​=5.556×10−6 m2⋅K/W

    Note that the above is the resistance of the interface.

    Thermal resistance of a plate is,

    Rcond​=kAL​

    Rcond′′​=kL​

    From Table A3,

    kCu​=401 W/m⋅K

    Required thickness to achieve the same resistance,

    Rcond′′​=Rtc′′​=kL​

    5.556×10−6=401L​

    L=0.0223 m=2.23 cm

    From the above result, the interface between two plates
    has as much resistance as a 2.23cm-thick copper plate.

    #Conduction in Cylinders and Spheres

    Consider steady heat conduction through a pipe.
    The wall of the pipe is very thin and temperature gradient in the radial direction is very large.

    From Fourier’s law of heat conduction,

    Q˙​cond,cyl​=−kAdrdT​

    Q˙​cond,cyl​=−k(2πrL)drdT​

    where A is the surface area of the cylinder

    Separating the variables and integrating,

    ∫r1​r2​​2πrLQ˙​cond,cyl​​ dr=∫T1​T2​​−k dT

    2πLQ˙​cond,cyl​​[ln(r2​)−ln(r1​)]=−k(T2​−T1​)

    2πLQ˙​cond,cyl​​⋅ln(r1​r2​​)=k(T1​−T2​)

    💡
    Q˙​cond,cyl​=2πLk⋅ln(r2​/r1​)T1​−T2​​

    Thermal resistance of a cylindrical body is defined as,

    💡
    Rcyl​=2πLkln(r2​/r1​)​

    where r2​ is outer radius and r1​ is inner radius

    Similarly, for a sphere,

    Q˙​cond,sph​=−k(4πr2)drdT​

    ∫r1​r2​​4πr2Q˙​cond,sph​​ dr=∫T1​T2​​−k dT

    4πQ˙​cond,sph​​(r1​1​−r2​1​)=−k(T2​−T1​)

    4πQ˙​cond,sph​​⋅r1​r2​r2​−r1​​=k(T1​−T2​)

    💡
    Q˙​cond,sph​=4πk(T1​−T2​)⋅r2​−r1​r1​r2​​

    Thermal resistance of a hollow sphere is defined as,

    💡
    Rsph​=4πr1​r2​kr2​−r1​​

    where r2​ is outer radius and r1​ is inner radius

    #Multi-layer Cylinders and Spheres

    Steady heat transfer through multi-layered cylinders and spheres can be determined
    by summing the thermal resistance of each layer, similar to a multi-layer plane wall.

    Consider a 3-layer composite cylinder subjected to convection on both sides.
    The total thermal resistance is the sum of the individual thermal resistances.

    Rtotal​=Rconv,1​+Rcyl,1​+Rcyl,2​+Rcyl,3​+Rconv,2​

    Rtotal​=h1​A1​1​+2πLk1​ln(r2​/r1​)​+2πLk2​ln(r3​/r2​)​+2πLk3​ln(r4​/r3​)​+h2​A4​1​

    where A1​ is the inner surface area, and A4​ is the outer surface area

    If Q˙​ is known, we can determine any intermediate temperature Tj​ using,

    💡
    Q˙​=Ri−j​Ti​−Tj​​

    where i−j follows the direction of steady heat transfer,
    and     Ri−j​ is the thermal resistance between locations i and j

    #Example 1

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1-dimensional heat transfer
    • Constant thermal conductivities
    • Negligible thermal contact resistance

    kFe​=80 W/m⋅K

    kwool​=0.05 W/m⋅K

    h1​=hsteam​=60 W/m2⋅K

    h2​=hcomb​=18 W/m2⋅K

    A1​=2π(0.025)(1)=0.157 m2 (inner surface)

    A3​=2π(0.0275+0.03)(1)=0.361 m2 (outer surface)

    Individual thermal resistances

    Convection resistance of steam,

    Ri​=Rconv,i​=h1​A1​1​=60(0.157)1​=0.106 K/W

    Conduction resistance of pipe,

    R1​=Rcyl​=2πLkFe​ln(r2​/r1​)​=2π(1)(80)ln(2.75/2.5)​=0.0002 K/W

    Conduction resistance of insulation,

    R2​=Rcyl​=2πLkwool​ln(r3​/r2​)​=2π(1)(0.05)ln(5.75/2.75)​=2.35 K/W

    Convection resistance of surroundings,

    Ro​=Rconv,2​=h2​A3​1​=18(0.361)1​=0.154 K/W

    Total thermal resistance,

    Rtot​=Ri​+R1​+R2​+Ro​

    Rtot​=0.106+0.0002+2.35+0.154

    Rtot​=2.61 K/W

    Steady rate of heat transfer from steam,

    Q˙​=Rtot​T∞1​​−T∞2​​​

    Q˙​=2.61320−5​

    Q˙​=121 W (per meter of pipe length)

    Temperature drop across pipe shell,

    ΔTpipe​=Q˙​Rpipe​=121(0.0002)=0.02 K

    Temperature drop across insulation,

    ΔTinsul​=Q˙​Rinsul​=121(2.35)=284 K

    #Example 2

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1-dimensional heat transfer
    • Constant thermal conductivity

    ksteel​=15 W/m⋅K

    h1​=80 W/m2⋅K

    h2​=10 W/m2⋅K

    A1​=4π(1.5)2=28.2 m2 (inner surface)

    A2​=4π(1.52)2=29.0 m2 (outer surface)

    Radiation heat transfer coefficient,

    hrad​=εσ(T2​2+T∞2​​2)(T2​+T∞2​​)

    Outer surface temperature of the tank is unknown. Thus, we need to
    assume a     T2​ value and check the accuracy of our assumption later.

    Assume T2​=5°C=278 K.

    Note that heat transfer coefficient inside of the tank is much larger.
    Thus,     T2​ must be closer to closer to 0°C, within the range 0°C to 22°C.

    hrad​=1(5.67×10−8)(2782+2952)(278+295)=5.34 W/m2⋅K

    Individual thermal resistances

    Ri​=Rconv,1​=h1​A1​1​=80(28.3)1​=0.000442 K/W

    R1​=Rsph​=4πr1​r2​kr2​−r1​​=4π(1.52)(1.5)(15)1.52−1.5​=0.000047 K/W

    Ro​=Rconv,2​=h2​A2​1​=10(29)1​=0.00345 K/W

    Rrad​=hrad​A2​1​=5.34(29)1​=0.00646 K/W

    Total thermal resistance,

    Rtot​=Ri​+R1​+1/Ro​+1/Rrad​1​

    Rtot​=0.000442+0.000047+0.00225

    Rtot​=0.00274 K/W

    Steady rate of heat transfer to iced water,

    Q˙​=Rtot​T∞2​​−T∞1​​​=0.0027422−0​=8029 W

    Note that direction of heat transfer is into the sphere (iced water).

    Outer surface temperature,

    Q˙​=1/Ro​+1/Rrad​1​T∞2​​−T2​​

    8029=0.00225295−T2​​

    T2​=276.93 K=3.93°C

    Since the assumed value is sufficiently close,
    there is no need to repeat the calculations.

    #Critical Radius of Insulation

    Adding insulation to a cylindrical pipe or a spherical shell will increase the conduction
    resistance of the insulation layer. However, it may decrease convection resistance of
    the surface since there is an increase in the outer surface area.

    Consider a cylindrical pipe of outer radius r1​.
    The pipe is insulated with a material with a
    thermal conductivity k and outer radius r2​.

    The rate of heat transfer from the pipe to
    the surrounding air can be expressed as,

    Q˙​=Rinsul​+Rconv​T1​−T∞​​

    Rinsul​=2πLkln(r2​/r1​)​

    Rconv​=h(2πr2​L)1​

    To minimize Q˙​, we need to maximize Rtotal​.

    dr2​dRtotal​​=dr2​d​[2πLk1n(r2​/r1​)​+h(2πr2​L)1​]=0

    dr2​dRtotal′​​=dr2​d​[2πkln(r2​/r1​)​+h(2πr2​)1​]=0

    Note that Rtotal′​ represents resistance for
    a unit length and has units     m⋅K/W.

    Solving the above equation,

    2πr2​k1​−2πr2​2h1​=0

    2πr2​k1​=2πr2​2h1​

    r2​=2πh2πk​

    Critical radius of insulation for a cylindrical pipe is,

    💡
    rcr,cyl​=hk​

    where k is thermal conductivity of the insulation,
    and     h is the external convection coefficient

    Critical radius of insulation for a hollow sphere is,

    💡
    rcr,sph​=h2k​

    For r<rcr​, rate of heat transfer increases with the addition of insulation.
    For r>rcr​, rate of heat transfer decreases with the addition of insulation.
    When r=rcr​, rate of heat transfer reaches a maximum.

    #Example

    Assumptions:

    • Steady-state heat transfer
    • 1-dimensional heat transfer
    • Constant thermal conductivity
    • Negligible contact thermal resistance
    • Heat transfer coefficient accounts for radiation

    kplastic​=0.15 W/m⋅K

    ho​=12 W/m2⋅K

    Q˙​=VI=8(10)=80 W (heat generated)

    A2​=2π(0.0035)(5)=0.11 m2 (outer surface)

    Convection resistance (outer surface),

    Ro​=Rconv​=ho​A2​1​=12(0.11)1​=0.76 K/W

    Conduction resistance of plastic,

    Rplastic​=Rcyl​=2πLkln(r2​/r1​)​=2π(5)(0.15)ln(3.5/1.5)​=0.18 K/W

    Total thermal resistance,

    Rtot​=Rplastic​+Ro​

    Rtot​=0.18+0.76

    Rtot​=0.94 K/W

    Temperature of interface,

    Q˙​=Rtot​T1​−T∞​​

    80=0.94T1​−303​

    T1​=378 K=105°C

    Critical radius of plastic insulation,

    rcr​=hk​=120.15​=0.0125 m=12.5 mm

    Since r2​<rcr​, increasing the thickness of the insulation will enhance
    heat transfer until the outer radius of the insulation reaches 12.5mm.

    #Heat Transfer from Extended Surfaces

    Newton’s law of cooling is given by,

    💡
    Q˙​conv​=hAs​(Ts​−T∞​)

    To increase the rate of heat transfer, it is easier to increase surface area by attaching to the surface extended surfaces — fins, made of highly conductive materials. Fins enhance heat transfer by exposing a larger surface area to convection and radiation.

    Assumptions for heat transfer in a fin:

    • Fin is thin (t≪w)
    • Steady-state and 1D heat transfer across the fin
    • Convection coefficient is uniform around the fin
    • Radiation is negligible

    Consider a volume element of a fin at location x
    have a length of Δx, a cross-sectional area Ac​
    and a perimeter p.

    Energy balance for the element is,

    Q˙​cond,x​=Q˙​cond,x+Δx​+Q˙​conv​

    Q˙​cond,x​=Q˙​cond,x+Δx​+h(p Δx)(T−T∞​)

    0=ΔxQ˙​cond,x+Δx​−Q˙​cond,x​​+hp(T−T∞​)

    0=dxdQ˙​cond​​+hp(T−T∞​)

    Note that p is perimeter of the cross section area.
    Note that temperature     T varies with location x.

    Substituting Fourier’s law of conduction,

    0=dxd​(−kAc​dxdT​)+hp(T−T∞​)

    💡
    0=dxd​(kAc​dxdT​)−hp(T−T∞​)

    For a fin with constant cross section and thermal conductivity,

    💡
    0=dx2d2T​−kAc​hp​(T−T∞​)0=dx2d2θ​−m2θ

    where excess temperature θ=T−T∞​ and m2=kAc​hp​

    General solution to the differential equation is,

    💡
    θ(x)=C1​emx+C2​e−mxθ(x)=C1​cosh(mx)+C2​sinh(mx)

    where C1​ and C2​ are determined from boundary conditions at the base and tip of the fin

    Temperature of the plate to which the fins are attached to is usually known.
    Thus, at the fin base, we have a specified temperature boundary condition.

    💡
    θ(0)=θb​=Tb​−T∞​

    #Boundary Conditions at Fin Tip

    Procedure for fin calculation:

    • If it is stated that the fin is infinite, or the fin tip has a specified temperature,
      or the fin has an adiabatic tip, use the respective equations for each scenario
    • If mL≥2.65 (for fin heat transfer) or mL≥4.6 (for fin
      heat transfer and fin temperature), use infinite fin equation
    • If the ratio Afin​Ac​​ is extremely small, use adiabatic fin equation
    • Else, use convective tip equation or approximate using Lc​

    #Infinitely Long Fin (Ttip​=T∞​)

    For a sufficiently long fin, the tip approaches the environment temperature T∞​.

    Boundary conditions:

    • θ(0)=θb​
    • θ(L→∞)=0

    Excess temperature distribution along the fin is,

    💡
    θb​θ​=Tb​−T∞​T−T∞​​=e−mx=e−xhp/kAc​​

    Note that temperature along the fin decreases exponentially from Tb​ to T∞​.

    Heat transfer from the base of the fin is,

    💡
    Q˙​fin​=hpkAc​​(Tb​−T∞​)

    #Adiabatic Fin Tip (Q˙​tip​=0)

    Heat transfer from the tip can be considered negligible since the
    surface area of the tip is usually much smaller than total fin area.

    Boundary conditions:

    • θ(0)=θb​
    • −kdxdθ​​x=L​=0 (Adiabatic surface condition)

    Excess temperature distribution along the fin is,

    💡
    θb​θ​=Tb​−T∞​T−T∞​​=cosh mLcosh m(L−x)​

    Heat transfer from the base of the fin is,

    💡
    Q˙​fin​=hpkAc​​(Tb​−T∞​)⋅tanh mL

    #Specified Temperature (Ttip​=TL​)

    The temperature of the fin tip is fixed at a specified temperature TL​.

    Boundary conditions:

    • θ(0)=θb​
    • θ(L)=θL​

    Excess temperature distribution along the fin is,

    💡
    θb​θ​=Tb​−T∞​T−T∞​​=sinh mL(θL​/θb​)sinh mx+sinh m(L−x)​

    Heat transfer from the base of the fin is,

    💡
    Q˙​fin​=hpkAc​​(Tb​−T∞​)⋅sinh mLcosh mL−(θL​/θb​)​

    #Convective Heat Loss at Fin Tip

    Fin tips are exposed to the surroundings, thus convection can occur as well.

    Boundary conditions:

    • θ(0)=θb​
    • −kdxdθ​​x=L​=hθL​ (convection boundary condition)

    Excess temperature distribution along the fin is,

    💡
    θb​θ​=Tb​−T∞​T−T∞​​=cosh mL+(h/mk)sinh mLcosh m(L−x)+(h/mk)sinh m(L−x)​

    Heat transfer from the base of the fin is,

    💡
    Q˙​fin​=hpkAc​​(Tb​−T∞​)⋅cosh mL+(h/mk)sinh mLsinh mL+(h/mk)cosh mL​

    #Proper Length of a Fin

    Temperature drops along the fin exponentially and reaches the environment temperature at some length. Thus, the part the fin beyond this length does not contribute to heat transfer since it is at the same temperature as the environment.

    To determine the proper length of a fin, compare heat transfer from a finite to that of an infinite fin.

    💡
    Q˙​long fin​Q˙​fin​​=hpkAc​​(Tb​−T∞​)hpkAc​​(Tb​−T∞​)⋅tanh mL​

    • Evaluate tanh mL for certain values of mL
    • Heat transfer increases linearly at first
    • Eventually converges to a value
    • Proper length of fin is L=mmL​

    In practice, a fin length that corresponds to about mL=1 will transfer 76.2% of the heat that can
    be transferred by an infinitely long fin.

    #Fin Effectiveness

    Fin effectiveness compares fin heat transfer against a base with no fin.

    Effectiveness of a fin is determined based on the increase
    in heat transfer the fin provides relative to the no-fin case.

    💡
    εfin​=Q˙​no fin​Q˙​fin​​=hAb​(Tb​−T∞​)Q˙​fin​​

    εfin​=1 indicates that adding fins does not affect heat transfer at all.
    εfin​<1 indicates that the fin acts as insulation (reduce heat transfer).
    εfin​>1 indicates that the fin increases heat transfer from the surface.

    Effectiveness of an infinitely long fin with a uniform cross-section is,

    💡
    εlong fin​=hAb​(Tb​−T∞​)hpkAc​​(Tb​−T∞​)​=hAc​kp​​

    If εfin​≥2, the addition of fins is beneficial.

    Fin effectiveness is enhance by:

    • Materials with high thermal conductivity k
    • High Ac​p​ ratio (thin but closely-spaced fins)
    • Medium with low convection coefficient

    Use of fins is more beneficial when the surrounding medium is a gas instead of a liquid, and the heat transfer is by natural convection instead of by
    forced convection.

    #Fin Efficiency

    Fin efficiency compares a fin with an ideal fin with no temperature drop.

    Temperature of the fin drops along its length. Thus, heat transfer from the fin is less due to decreasing temperature difference T(x)−T∞​.

    Maximum heat transfer from the fin is,

    💡
    Q˙​fin,max​=hAfin​(Tb​−T∞​)

    Heat which would be transferred if the entire
    fin was at the same temperature as its base.

    Fin efficiency is defined as,

    💡
    ηfin​=Q˙​fin,max​Q˙​fin​​=hAfin​(Tb​−T∞​)Q˙​fin​​

    where Afin​ is total surface area of fin

    Efficiency of a fin with an adiabatic tip,

    💡
    ηadiab​=mLtanh mL​

    Note that efficiency of other fin configurations
    can be found in Table 3-3 of the textbook.

    #Corrected Fin Length

    Efficiency of a fin with convective heat loss at
    the tip can be approximated by treating it as
    an adiabatic tip using a corrected length.

    💡
    Lc​=L+pAc​​

    For a rectangular cross-section fin,

    💡
    Lc,rect​=L+2t​

    where t is the thickness of the rectangular fins

    For a cylindrical cross-section fin,

    💡
    Lc,cyl​=L+4D​

    where D is the diameter of the cylindrical fins

    For a rectangular fin, if 2kht​<0.0625, use Lc,rect​.

    For a pin fin, if 2khD​<0.0625, use Lc,cyl​.

    Efficiency of a fin with convective heat loss at the tip can be computed
    by replacing L with Lc​ in the equation for a fin with an adiabatic tip.

    💡
    ηfin​=mLc​tanh mLc​​

    #Thermal Resistance

    Rearranging the efficiency equation, the thermal resistance of a fin is,

    💡
    Rfin​=Q˙​fin​Tb​−T∞​​=hAfin​ηfin​1​

    Note that R accounts for both conduction along the fin and convection into the fluid.

    #Overall Efficiency

    For a surface with multiple fins, heat transfer is from both the fins and the un-finned surfaces.

    Overall surface efficiency is defined as,

    💡
    ηo​=Q˙​max​Q˙​tot​​=hAtot​(Tb​−T∞​)Q˙​tot​​

    where Atot​ is total exposed area
    of the fin and un-finned surfaces

    Alternative equation,

    Q˙​tot​=Q˙​fin​+Q˙​unfin​

    Q˙​tot​=ηfin​hAfin​θb​+hAb​θb​

    Q˙​tot​=hθb​(ηfin​Afin​+Ab​)

    Q˙​tot​=hθb​[ηfin​Afin​+(Atot​−Afin​)]

    Q˙​tot​=hAtot​θb​[1−Atot​Afin​​(1−ηfin​)]

    💡
    ηo​=1−Atot​Afin​​(1−ηfin​)

    Note that Afin​ is total surface area of the fins.
